summaries.example: Imagine throwing a stone. While your hand touches it, your hand helps make it move. Medieval thinkers then asked: what keeps it moving after it leaves your hand? Some said the air helped push it. Others, such as Buridan and Oresme, said the stone received an inner moving power called impetus, which slowly faded.
summaries.summary: Medieval philosophers studied causation because they wanted to understand the changing world and its relation to God. They discussed motion in a broad sense: not only travel from place to place, but also changes such as growing, learning, choosing, and becoming stronger or weaker. Many followed Aristotle’s picture of things as combinations of matter and form. Form was more than shape; it helped explain what a thing could do. Thinkers debated how an agent causes change in a patient, or receiver of change. They also argued about natural motion, thrown objects, the will, perception, necessity, and purposes in nature. Buridan and Oresme criticized Aristotle’s account of projectile motion and used impetus to explain continued movement. These debates show that medieval theories were varied and often inventive, even while they shared important basic assumptions.
key_ideas: Medieval philosophers asked how things change, move, sense, choose, and come to be known.
They often used ideas from Aristotle, but they did not all agree with Aristotle or with one another.
Many thinkers viewed things as made from matter and form. A thing’s form helped explain its powers and actions.
Some philosophers criticized Aristotle’s explanation of thrown objects and proposed impetus instead.
Questions about causes were connected to questions about God, free choice, knowledge, and purpose in nature.
summaries.why_it_matters: Studying these ideas shows that people have long asked careful questions about change and explanation. It also shows how one question can connect to many others: how a stone moves can lead to questions about what things are, how minds choose, how people know the world, and whether nature has purposes. Medieval debates helped develop detailed ways of thinking about continuous change.

important_terms.definition: An explanation of why something happens or changes.
A change of state, such as growing, becoming warmer, or moving from one place to another.
A built-in tendency thought to guide a thing toward its proper result or place.
A moving power thought to remain in a thrown object and gradually weaken.
The material part of a thing, joined with its form.
The active principle that helps make a thing the kind of thing it is and helps explain what it can do.

questions_to_think_about: What might keep a ball moving after it leaves your hand?
Can something change because of its own power, or must something else always change it?
Is a goal or purpose needed to explain how a plant grows?
Why might a philosopher’s ideas about what exists affect their explanation of what happens?

summaries.example: Consider a projectile after release. Aristotle’s account appealed to the surrounding air and a temporary absence behind the moving object, but critics argued that this did not fit cases such as a heavier stone being easier to throw than a light bean or two stones passing close to each other. Buridan and Oresme instead appealed to impetus, an inhering form that drives the projectile and diminishes over time. Their proposal changed the explanation of motion without abandoning the broader medieval ontology of forms in substances and active and passive roles in causal interaction.
summaries.summary: The medieval study of causation was not a single doctrine but a set of debates shaped by Aristotelian physics, theology, and theories of mind. “Motion” included general change of state as well as local movement. Medieval authors analyzed how an agent produces change in a patient and often explained causal powers through hylomorphism: substances were composites of matter and form, and form was an active principle rather than merely a shape. This framework supported detailed accounts of continuous variation, including debates later connected with the development of calculus. It also persisted in revised explanations. Buridan and Oresme criticized Aristotle’s account of projectile motion and appealed to impetus, but impetus was still a form inhering in a substance. Discussions of will tested whether all change must be caused by something other than the changing thing; Scotus and Ockham defended important forms of self-determination. Debates over perception concerned species, relational accounts, and Ockham’s action-at-a-distance alternative. Finally, medieval writers distinguished causal necessity from knowledge of causal propositions, and efficient causes from final causes. The entry emphasizes that these positions cannot simply be labeled modern or Humean: their terms and problems belong to a different conceptual setting.
key_ideas: Medieval causal theories developed through engagement with Aristotle, especially the Physics, but also through theological and philosophical concerns about creation, grace, will, perception, and freedom.
In the dominant hylomorphic framework, forms were active principles responsible for causal powers, while causal interactions generally assigned active and passive roles to substances.
Aristotle’s account of projectile motion faced medieval objections. Buridan and Oresme used impetus to explain continued motion, yet their account remained form-based rather than fully Newtonian.

Theories of the will raised a conflict between natural determination and self-determination. Scotus distinguished natural causes from a will capable of choosing otherwise under identical circumstances.

Medieval authors disagreed about whether perception required intermediary species, and Ockham rejected species in favor of accounts involving action at a distance. These proposals depended partly on assumptions about what entities exist.

Medieval discussions separated the metaphysical question of whether causal connections are necessary from the epistemological question of whether causal propositions can be known, including through experience and demonstration.
summaries.why_it_matters: These theories matter because they reveal how explanations depend on background assumptions about reality. A change in ontology—what entities and powers one accepts—can reshape accounts of motion, perception, agency, and scientific knowledge. The medieval discussions also show that criticism of an older theory does not necessarily produce a completely modern one: Buridan and Oresme revised projectile theory while retaining important hylomorphic commitments. Their work is therefore useful for understanding both continuity and change in the history of philosophy and science.

important_terms.definition: A relation or explanatory connection through which one event, state, or entity brings about or helps explain another.
In Aristotelian physics, change in a broad sense, including alteration and change of place; local motion is only one kind.
The view that substances are compounds of matter and form, with form functioning as an active principle in a thing’s causal powers.
A causal role assigned to what brings about a change; the recipient of the change is the patient.
An internal form or power proposed by Buridan and Oresme to explain a projectile’s continued non-natural motion, with a tendency to decay.
A change directed toward an end or purpose, especially in explanations of natural processes such as growth.
The distinction between God’s unrestricted ability to create possibilities and the more limited power exercised according to an ordered, just will.
A proof in which causal structure is central; a proof of the reasoned fact uses a cause as the explanatory middle term.

questions_to_think_about: Does replacing Aristotle’s explanation of projectile motion with impetus change the underlying theory of what kinds of things have causal powers?
If a will can choose otherwise under exactly the same circumstances, how does that differ from a natural cause?
Can an explanation be simpler merely because it assumes fewer entities? What might be lost by removing species from perception?
How should we distinguish a causal relation in the world from our evidence or argument for believing in it?
Can growth or other natural processes be explained by ends, or only by efficient causes?

summaries.example: Suppose you kick a soccer ball. Your foot clearly affects the ball while they touch. But why does the ball continue afterward? Aristotle’s explanation appealed to the air around the ball, yet medieval critics found problems with it. Buridan and Oresme proposed that the ball receives impetus, an inner moving power that gradually weakens. This idea offered a different causal story, although it still treated powers as forms belonging to things.
summaries.summary: Medieval theories of causation grew from close study of Aristotle as well as from questions about God, nature, ethics, freedom, and knowledge. Medieval philosophers used “motion” broadly, meaning many kinds of change, not only movement across a room. They often worked within hylomorphism, the view that substances combine matter and form. Form was not just outward shape; it helped explain a thing’s powers and causal activities. This framework led to detailed arguments about how forms become stronger or weaker over continuous changes. It also shaped debates about projectile motion. Aristotle’s explanation of a thrown object’s continued movement faced objections, and Buridan and Oresme proposed impetus, a form or power that remains in the object and declines. Yet this was still different from later accounts that treat rest and steady motion in a more equal way. Other debates concerned whether the will can move itself, whether perception requires species between objects and knowers, whether causal relations are necessary, and how causal knowledge can be demonstrated. Medieval thinkers also disagreed about final causes, or purposes in nature.
key_ideas: Medieval philosophers studied causes partly because they wanted to understand nature, the human mind, freedom, and the relation between the world and God.
Their idea of motion was broad. It included changes in qualities and states, so it could be used to study continuous change.
Aristotle’s ideas were influential, but medieval thinkers argued over how change occurs and how projectiles keep moving after contact ends.
Buridan and Oresme used impetus to challenge Aristotle’s projectile theory. Their account was innovative but still relied on forms within substances.
Debates about the will asked whether a person can determine an action or whether desires and goals settle the action in advance.
Different views of perception depended on different beliefs about whether mental or sensory likenesses, called species, really exist.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic matters because it connects questions that are often studied separately today. Ideas about what a thing is affected ideas about how it acts; ideas about causation affected theories of freedom, perception, science, and nature’s purposes. The history also cautions us not to treat medieval philosophy as one fixed view or to assume that a criticism of Aristotle immediately produced modern science.

important_terms.definition: The connection that explains how one thing, event, or change brings about another.
Any change of state, including growth or becoming different, not just movement from one location to another.
The idea that things are made of matter and form, and that form helps explain their abilities and effects.
A thing that produces a change; the patient is the thing that receives or undergoes the change.
An internal moving power used by some medieval thinkers to explain why a thrown object keeps moving.
An explanation that refers to a goal or purpose, such as a natural process tending toward a completed state.
The ability to choose freely rather than being forced by an end or by ordinary natural causes.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a theory of motion include changes such as becoming warmer or more skilled?
Does an inner power like impetus explain motion better than a theory based on surrounding air?
If a person can choose otherwise in the same situation, what does that suggest about freedom?
How could beliefs about what exists affect a theory of seeing or remembering?
Are goals useful explanations for natural events, or only for actions by thinking beings?
